```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggthemes)
library(ggpubr)
library(latex2exp)

path = 'Data/'

fmt <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(x, format = 'f', digits = d)
tab <- function(df, ...) kable(df, format = 'html', row.names = FALSE, escape = FALSE, ...) %>%
  kable_classic(full_width = FALSE, html_font = "Cambria") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = 'striped')
near <- function(a, b, tol = 5e-4) abs(a - b) < tol
notes_theme <- theme_classic2() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 11), axis.title = element_text(size = 13),
        strip.text = element_text(size = 13, face = 'bold'), strip.background = element_blank())

# every number quoted on this page is computed here. The slide numbers are the same
# ones asserted in assets/make_lecture18_figures.R.

# spinner: X = 1, 2, 3 each with probability 1/3; x-bar of n = 2 spins
sp <- expand.grid(a = 1:3, b = 1:3)
sp$m <- (sp$a + sp$b) / 2
spd <- aggregate(list(count = rep(1, 9)), list(m = sp$m), sum)
spd$p <- spd$count / 9
s_sd <- sqrt(mean(((1:3) - 2)^2)); sb_sd <- sqrt(sum((spd$m - 2)^2 * spd$p))
stopifnot(identical(spd$count, c(1, 2, 3, 2, 1)), near(sum(spd$m * spd$p), 2, 1e-12),
          near(s_sd, 0.82, 5e-3), near(sb_sd, 0.58, 5e-3), near(sb_sd, s_sd / sqrt(2), 1e-12))

# Coho salmon (kept from the 2024 notes): the mean of n = 3 afternoons, all 27 outcomes
cx <- 0:2; cp <- c(0.589, 0.232, 0.179)
grid <- expand.grid(a = 1:3, b = 1:3, c = 1:3)
gs <- cx[grid$a] + cx[grid$b] + cx[grid$c]           # total catch; x-bar = total / 3
gp <- cp[grid$a] * cp[grid$b] * cp[grid$c]
coho <- aggregate(gp, list(total = gs), sum)
coho$xbar <- coho$total / 3
c_mu <- sum(cx * cp); c_sd <- sqrt(sum((cx - c_mu)^2 * cp))
cb_mu <- sum(coho$xbar * coho$x); cb_sd <- sqrt(sum((coho$xbar - cb_mu)^2 * coho$x))
stopifnot(abs(sum(cp) - 1) < 1e-12, nrow(coho) == 7,
          all(abs(coho$x - c(0.204, 0.241, 0.281, 0.159, 0.085, 0.022, 0.006)) < 6e-4),
          abs(cb_mu - c_mu) < 1e-12, abs(cb_sd - c_sd / sqrt(3)) < 1e-12)

# Spotify songs: the population for the standard-error and confidence-interval examples.
# A song credited to several artists appears once per artist in the file, so duplicates
# by Spotify URI are dropped.
sg <- read.csv(paste0(path, 'Spotify_Youtube.csv'), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
stopifnot(nrow(sg) == 20718, length(unique(sg$Artist)) == 2079)
sg <- sg[!duplicated(sg$Uri) & !is.na(sg$Duration_ms), ]
x <- sg$Duration_ms / 60000
MU <- mean(x); SIG <- sd(x)
stopifnot(length(x) == 18860, round(MU, 2) == 3.71, round(SIG, 2) == 1.51,
          round(median(x), 2) == 3.55, sum(x > 10) == 41, round(max(x)) == 78,
          near(1.51 / sqrt(20), 0.34, 5e-3), near(1.51 / sqrt(80), 0.17, 5e-3),
          identical(round(x[1:5], 2), c(3.71, 3.34, 3.59, 3.90, 5.68)))
set.seed(10)                                   # the 25 intervals on the Lecture 18 slide
cm <- replicate(25, mean(sample(x, 20, replace = TRUE)))
ci <- data.frame(i = 1:25, m = cm, lo = cm - 2 * 0.34, hi = cm + 2 * 0.34)
ci$hit <- ci$lo <= MU & MU <= ci$hi
stopifnot(sum(ci$hit) == 24, round(cm[1], 2) == 3.64, ci$hit[1],
          near(3.64 - 0.68, 2.96, 1e-9), near(3.64 + 0.68, 4.32, 1e-9))
set.seed(1)                                    # the long-run capture rate
cover <- mean(replicate(10000, abs(mean(sample(x, 20, replace = TRUE)) - MU) <= 2 * SIG / sqrt(20)))
set.seed(1)
cover200 <- mean(replicate(10000, abs(mean(sample(x, 200, replace = TRUE)) - MU) <= 2 * SIG / sqrt(200)))
stopifnot(cover > 0.975, cover < 0.99, cover200 > 0.94, cover200 < 0.965)

# minutes until the next goal: simulated at the 2022 World Cup rate (same as Lecture 18)
lam <- 172 / 64
gap <- 90 / 2.69          # the rounded rate, as in make_lecture18_figures.R, so the waits match the slide
set.seed(7)
clt_n <- c(1, 2, 5, 30)
clt <- do.call(rbind, lapply(clt_n, function(n)
  data.frame(n = paste0('n = ', n), m = replicate(10000, mean(rexp(n, 1 / gap))))))
stopifnot(identical(round(clt$m[1:5], 1), c(1.6, 54.3, 57.3, 27.2, 18.3)))
clt$n <- factor(clt$n, levels = paste0('n = ', clt_n))
chk <- tapply(clt$m, clt$n, sd) / (gap / sqrt(clt_n))
stopifnot(near(lam, 2.69, 5e-3), near(gap, 33.5, 0.05),
          all(abs(tapply(clt$m, clt$n, mean) - gap) < 0.6), all(abs(chk - 1) < 0.03))

# Stephen Curry's free throws: exact sampling distributions of p-hat
p_ft <- 4236 / 4645
ph_n <- c(10, 30, 100)
ph <- do.call(rbind, lapply(ph_n, function(n)
  data.frame(n = paste0('n = ', n), ph = (0:n) / n, p = dbinom(0:n, n, 0.912), w = 0.7 / n)))
ph$n <- factor(ph$n, levels = paste0('n = ', ph_n))
se_ft <- sqrt(0.912 * 0.088 / 100)
stopifnot(near(p_ft, 0.912), near(se_ft, 0.028, 5e-4),
          near(c(10, 30, 100) * 0.088, c(0.88, 2.64, 8.8), 1e-9),
          near(0.912 - 2 * 0.028, 0.856, 1e-9), near(0.912 + 2 * 0.028, 0.968, 1e-9))

# World Cup tournament average over 64 matches
se_wc <- sqrt(lam) / sqrt(64)
z3 <- (3 - 2.69) / 0.205
stopifnot(near(sqrt(lam), 1.64, 5e-3), near(se_wc, 0.205, 5e-4),
          near(2.69 - 2 * 0.205, 2.28, 1e-9), near(2.69 + 2 * 0.205, 3.10, 1e-9),
          near(169 / 64, 2.64, 5e-3), round(z3, 2) == 1.51,
          round(1 - pnorm(1.51), 3) == 0.066, round(1 - ppois(191, 64 * lam), 2) == 0.07)
```

# Sampling distributions

## Two polls, two answers

Two polling firms each survey a random sample of 1,000 voters in the same state, in the same week.
Poll A finds that $\hat{p} = 0.52$ of voters support a ballot measure; Poll B finds $\hat{p} = 0.49$.
Is one of the polls wrong?

Not necessarily. Different random samples contain different people, so they give different values of
$\hat{p}$. This is the sampling variation we met in Week 6. Now imagine 1,000 firms each polling 1,000
voters: their 1,000 values of $\hat{p}$ would pile up around the true proportion $p$, and the shape
of that pile tells us how far any one poll is likely to be from the truth. This week is about that
pile.

## Three distributions

A statistic computed from a random sample or a randomized experiment is a **random variable**: its
value depends on which units chance put in the sample, so it has a probability distribution of its
own. We now have three distributions to keep apart:

* The **population distribution** is the probability distribution of a single observation $X$. Its
  properties are described by **parameters** such as $\mu$, $\sigma$ and $p$, which we usually do
  not know.
* The **data distribution** is the distribution of the $n$ observations in our one sample, the
  histogram of our data. Its properties are described by **statistics** such as $\bar{x}$, $s$ and
  $\hat{p}$.
* The **sampling distribution** is the probability distribution of a statistic, such as $\bar{x}$
  or $\hat{p}$, over all possible samples of the same size $n$ from the same population. It tells us
  how close an estimate is likely to be to the parameter it estimates.

## Building a sampling distribution by hand

For a discrete population and a small sample we can find a sampling distribution exactly, with the
probability rules from Week 6:

1. List every possible sample of size $n$ and compute the statistic for each.
2. Find the probability of each sample. When the observations are independent, multiply.
3. Add up the probabilities of the samples that give the same value of the statistic.

### Example: a spinner

A spinner lands on 1, 2 or 3, each with probability 1/3, so the population has $\mu = 2$. Spin it
twice and record the mean of the two spins, $\bar{x}$. There are $3 \times 3 = 9$ equally likely
samples, and **order matters**: (1, 2) and (2, 1) are different samples.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
tab(data.frame(
  xbar = c('1', '1.5', '2', '2.5', '3'),
  samples = c('(1,1)', '(1,2), (2,1)', '(1,3), (2,2), (3,1)', '(2,3), (3,2)', '(3,3)'),
  p = c('1/9', '2/9', '3/9', '2/9', '1/9')),
  col.names = c('$\\bar{x}$', 'Samples giving it', '$P(\\bar{x})$'))
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.height=3.4, fig.width=10, fig.align='center', fig.alt = "Two bar charts side by side. Left, one spin X: three equal bars of height one third at 1, 2 and 3. Right, the mean of two spins x-bar: five bars at 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5 and 3 with heights 1/9, 2/9, 3/9, 2/9 and 1/9, peaked in the middle at 2."}
spall <- rbind(data.frame(m = 1:3, p = 1 / 3, lab = '1/3', panel = 'One spin:  X', w = 0.5),
               data.frame(m = spd$m, p = spd$p, lab = paste0(spd$count, '/9'),
                          panel = 'Mean of two spins:  x̄', w = 0.3))
spall$panel <- factor(spall$panel, levels = unique(spall$panel))
ggplot(spall, aes(m, p)) +
  geom_col(aes(width = w), fill = 'lightblue', color = 'black', linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_text(aes(label = lab), vjust = -0.4, size = 4.5) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3)) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 0.42)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = 'Probability') + notes_theme
```

Compare the population (left) with the sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$ (right):

* **Same center.** Both have mean 2.
* **Smaller spread.** One spin has $\sigma = `r fmt(s_sd, 2)`$; the mean of two spins has
  $\sigma_{\bar{x}} = `r fmt(sb_sd, 2)`$, which is exactly $`r fmt(s_sd, 2)`/\sqrt{2}$.
* **New shape.** The population is flat; the sampling distribution is already peaked in the
  middle, because a mean of 1 or 3 needs *both* spins to be extreme.

### Example: Coho salmon

Let $X$ be the number of Coho salmon a fly fisherman catches in an afternoon on the Clearwater River,
with this (hypothetical) population distribution:

```{r, echo=FALSE}
tab(data.frame(x = cx, p = fmt(cp, 3)), col.names = c('$x$', '$P(x)$'))
```

Its mean is $\mu = 0(0.589) + 1(0.232) + 2(0.179) = `r fmt(c_mu, 2)`$ fish and its standard deviation
is $\sigma = `r fmt(c_sd, 3)`$. Now find the sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$, the mean catch over
a random sample of $n = 3$ afternoons. This time the outcomes are not equally likely, so each sample's
probability comes from the multiplication rule. There are $3 \times 3 \times 3 = 27$ possible
samples:

```{r, echo=FALSE}
tab(data.frame(
  xbar = c('0', '1/3', '2/3', '1', '4/3', '5/3', '2'),
  outs = c('(0,0,0) = $\\color{red}{1}$',
           '(1,0,0), (0,1,0), (0,0,1) = $\\color{red}{3}$',
           '(1,1,0), (1,0,1), (0,1,1), (2,0,0), (0,2,0), (0,0,2) = $\\color{red}{6}$',
           '(1,1,1), (2,1,0), (2,0,1), (0,2,1), (1,2,0), (1,0,2), (0,1,2) = $\\color{red}{7}$',
           '(2,1,1), (1,2,1), (1,1,2), (2,2,0), (2,0,2), (0,2,2) = $\\color{red}{6}$',
           '(1,2,2), (2,1,2), (2,2,1) = $\\color{red}{3}$',
           '(2,2,2) = $\\color{red}{1}$'),
  calc = c('$0.589^3$',
           '$3(0.589^2 \\times 0.232)$',
           '$3(0.232^2 \\times 0.589) + 3(0.589^2 \\times 0.179)$',
           '$0.232^3 + 6(0.589 \\times 0.232 \\times 0.179)$',
           '$3(0.232^2 \\times 0.179) + 3(0.179^2 \\times 0.589)$',
           '$3(0.179^2 \\times 0.232)$',
           '$0.179^3$'),
  p = paste0('$\\color{red}{', fmt(coho$x, 3), '}$')),
  col.names = c('$\\bar{x}$', 'Samples giving it', 'Probability', '$P(\\bar{x})$'))
```

The counts in red add to 27 and the probabilities add to 1. Once again:

* the mean of the sampling distribution is $\mu_{\bar{x}} = \sum \bar{x}\, P(\bar{x}) = `r fmt(cb_mu, 2)`$,
  **the same as** $\mu$;
* its standard deviation is $\sigma_{\bar{x}} = `r fmt(cb_sd, 3)`$, which is exactly
  $\sigma/\sqrt{n} = `r fmt(c_sd, 3)`/\sqrt{3}$.

## Center and spread of a sampling distribution

Those two examples are not coincidences. For a random sample of size $n$ from a population with
mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$:

* **The sample mean** $\bar{x}$ has mean $\mu_{\bar{x}} = \mu$: it is centered at the parameter it
  estimates. Its standard deviation is
  $$\sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$$
  the **standard error of the mean**, the same standard error we met in Week 6.

A **sample proportion** $\hat{p}$ is a sample mean too. Code each observation as a Bernoulli trial,
1 for a success and 0 for a failure; then $\hat{p}$ is the mean of the 0s and 1s, the count of
successes $X \sim \text{Binom}(n, p)$ divided by $n$. A Bernoulli population has mean $p$ and standard
deviation $\sqrt{p(1 - p)}$, so:

* **The sample proportion** $\hat{p} = X/n$ has mean $\mu_{\hat{p}} = p$ and standard error
  $$\sigma_{\hat{p}} = \sqrt{\frac{p(1 - p)}{n}}$$

Both statistics are **unbiased** (centered at the parameter), and both standard errors shrink like
$1/\sqrt{n}$.

### The data: Spotify songs

Spotify and YouTube statistics for the top 10 Spotify songs of each of 2,079 popular artists were
collected in February 2023. A song credited to several artists appears once for each of them, so we
count each song once, which leaves 18,860 different songs. Our variable is

* $X$ = the length of a song, in minutes.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
tab(rbind(data.frame(Track = sg$Track[1:5], Artist = sg$Artist[1:5], Minutes = fmt(x[1:5], 2)),
          data.frame(Track = '…', Artist = '…', Minutes = '…')))
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.height=3.6, fig.width=10, fig.align='center', fig.alt = "Histogram of the lengths of 18,860 Spotify songs from 0 to 10 minutes, with a vertical line at the mean of 3.71 minutes. Most songs are between 2.5 and 5 minutes, peaking around 3.5; the right tail is longer than the left. 41 songs longer than 10 minutes are off the right edge of the plot."}
ggplot(data.frame(x = x[x <= 10]), aes(x)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.2, boundary = 0, fill = 'lightgrey', color = 'black', linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = MU, color = 'red', linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:10) +
  labs(x = 'Song length (minutes)', y = 'Number of songs') + notes_theme
```

Most songs run between about 2.5 and 5 minutes, but the right tail is long: `r sum(x > 10)` songs
(mostly non-stop remix medleys and sleep sounds) are over 10 minutes, the longest
`r round(max(x))` minutes. Those are left off the plot so the rest is visible. Treating all
`r format(length(x), big.mark = ',')` songs as the population, $\mu = `r fmt(MU, 2)`$ minutes and
$\sigma = `r fmt(SIG, 2)`$ minutes.

### Example: standard error and $n$

Draw a random sample of $n$ songs and average their lengths to get $\bar{x}$. Every new sample gives a
different $\bar{x}$, and the standard error $\sigma_{\bar{x}}$ measures how much $\bar{x}$ varies from
sample to sample.

* For $n = 20$: $\sigma_{\bar{x}} = 1.51/\sqrt{20} \approx 0.34$ minutes.
* For $n = 80$: $\sigma_{\bar{x}} = 1.51/\sqrt{80} \approx 0.17$ minutes.

A single song is typically about 1.5 minutes from the mean; the average of 20 songs is typically only
about a third of a minute from it. And because $n$ sits under a square root, making the sample **4
times larger** only cuts the standard error **in half** ($\sqrt{4} = 2$).

# The central limit theorem

The formulas above give the center and spread of a sampling distribution. The **central limit
theorem** (CLT) gives its shape, and it is one of the most famous results in all of probability.

## Averaging a skewed variable

### The data: waiting for a goal

The 2022 World Cup produced 172 goals in its 64 matches, 2.69 goals per 90-minute match. If goals
arrive at that rate, independently of one another, then

* $X$ = minutes until the next goal

has mean $\mu = 90/2.69 \approx `r fmt(gap, 1)`$ minutes and, for this kind of waiting time, standard
deviation $\sigma \approx `r fmt(gap, 1)`$ minutes as well. These waits are **simulated** at the World
Cup rate, not recorded from matches. Here are the first five:

```{r, echo=FALSE}
tab(data.frame(Wait = c(1:5, '…'), Minutes = c(fmt(clt$m[1:5], 1), '…')))
```

Most waits are short and a few are very long, so $X$ is strongly skewed right. Now draw $n$ waits,
average them to get $\bar{x}$, and repeat 10,000 times. Each panel shows the 10,000 values of
$\bar{x}$ for one sample size:

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.height=3.6, fig.width=11, fig.align='center', fig.alt = "Four histograms of 10,000 simulated sample means of minutes until the next goal, for n = 1, 2, 5 and 30, each with a vertical line at the mean of about 33.5 minutes and its own axis scale. At n = 1 the histogram is strongly skewed right; the skew fades as n grows, and at n = 30 it is a narrow, nearly symmetric bell."}
ggplot(clt, aes(m)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 40, color = 'black', fill = 'lightblue', linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = gap, color = 'red', linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~n, nrow = 1, scales = 'free') +
  labs(x = TeX('Sample mean $\\bar{x}$ (minutes until the next goal)'), y = 'Density') +
  notes_theme + theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 10))
```

With $n = 1$ the "sample mean" is a single wait, so the first panel is the skewed population itself.
As $n$ grows:

* **Shape:** the skew fades into a bell. By $n = 30$ it is close to symmetric.
* **Center:** stays at $\mu = `r fmt(gap, 1)`$ (the red line).
* **Spread:** shrinks, just as $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$ says. Notice the axes: the values of $\bar{x}$
  run out past 400 minutes for $n = 1$ but stay between about 20 and 60 for $n = 30$.

## The theorem

* **Central limit theorem.** Take random samples of size $n$ from **any** population with mean $\mu$
  and standard deviation $\sigma$. If $n$ is large enough, the sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$ is
  approximately normal:
  $$\bar{x} \sim N\!\left(\mu,\; \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right)$$
  The larger $n$ is, the better the approximation. Since $\hat{p}$ is a sample mean of 0s and 1s, the
  same is true of it:
  $$\hat{p} \sim N\!\left(p,\; \sqrt{\frac{p(1 - p)}{n}}\right)$$

The remarkable part is "**any** population". The population can be skewed, lumpy or discrete; the
average of enough independent observations is still bell shaped, because the unusually high and
unusually low values in a sample cancel out. In Week 6 we saw the same thing with averages of dice.

**How large is large enough?** The textbook's guides are:

* $n \geq 30$ for $\bar{x}$. If the population is itself close to normal, much smaller samples will
  do; if it is very skewed or has extreme outliers, you may need more.
* $np > 5$ and $n(1 - p) > 5$ for $\hat{p}$: enough expected successes *and* failures.

> **For the curious: the formal statement.** For independent observations $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$
> from the same distribution, with mean $\mu$ and a finite standard deviation $\sigma$,
> $$\frac{\sqrt{n}\,(\bar{X} - \mu)}{\sigma} \xrightarrow{d} N(0, 1)$$
> where $\xrightarrow{d}$ means "converges in distribution". The left side is just the $z$-score of
> $\bar{X}$, so the theorem says that $z$-score behaves more and more like a standard normal $Z$ as
> $n$ grows. Notice the two assumptions: the observations come from the *same* distribution, and its
> variance is finite.

## The CLT for a proportion

Stephen Curry has made `r format(4236, big.mark = ',')` of his `r format(4645, big.mark = ',')`
career free throws, so take $p = 0.912$. Let $\hat{p}$ be the proportion he makes over a stretch of
$n$ free throws. Below are the **exact** sampling distributions of $\hat{p}$ (from the binomial
distribution) for $n = 10$, 30 and 100:

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.height=3.6, fig.width=11, fig.align='center', fig.alt = "Three bar charts of the exact sampling distribution of the proportion of free throws made, with p = 0.912 marked by a vertical line, each with its own axis scale. For n = 10 the bars are piled against 1 and strongly skewed left. For n = 30 they are still skewed left. For n = 100 they form a nearly symmetric bell centered at 0.912."}
ggplot(ph[ph$p > 1e-3, ], aes(ph, p)) +
  geom_col(aes(width = w), fill = 'lightblue', color = 'black', linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.912, color = 'red', linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~n, nrow = 1, scales = 'free') +
  labs(x = TeX('Sample proportion $\\hat{p}$ of free throws made'), y = 'Probability') +
  notes_theme + theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 10))
```

Check the rule: $n(1 - p) = 10(0.088) = 0.88$, $30(0.088) = 2.64$ and $100(0.088) = 8.8$. Only
$n = 100$ passes, and only $n = 100$ looks like a bell. With a success rate this high, misses are
the rare outcome, and you need enough of them for the distribution to fill out.

# Using the central limit theorem

Because the sampling distribution is approximately normal, everything we know about the normal
distribution applies to it. In particular, the empirical rule says about 95% of the area lies within
2 standard deviations of the mean:

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.height=2.8, fig.width=9, fig.align='center', fig.alt = "A normal curve for the sampling distribution of x-bar, with the x-axis labeled mu minus 2 sigma over root n, mu, and mu plus 2 sigma over root n. The area between the two outer labels is shaded and marked 0.95."}
ggplot(data.frame(x = c(-4, 4)), aes(x)) +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, linewidth = 1) +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, xlim = c(-2, 2), geom = 'area', fill = 'red1', alpha = 0.3) +
  annotate('text', x = 0, y = dnorm(0) / 2, label = '0.95', size = 9) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-2, 0, 2),
                     labels = c(TeX('$\\mu - 2\\sigma/\\sqrt{n}$'), TeX('$\\mu$'),
                                TeX('$\\mu + 2\\sigma/\\sqrt{n}$'))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 14), axis.title.x = element_text(size = 14),
        axis.text.y = element_blank(), axis.ticks.y = element_blank(), axis.line.y = element_blank())
```

So for the sample mean,

$$P\left(\mu - 2\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} \;\leq\; \bar{x} \;\leq\; \mu + 2\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right) \approx 0.95$$

and for the sample proportion,

$$P\left(p - 2\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}} \;\leq\; \hat{p} \;\leq\; p + 2\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}\right) \approx 0.95$$

In words: there is about a 95% probability that the statistic lands within **2 standard errors** of
the parameter. That distance is the **margin of error** from Week 6, now with a probability attached
to it.

### Example: free throws, again

Over a stretch of $n = 100$ free throws, let $\hat{p}$ be the proportion Curry makes. We checked that
$n(1 - p) = 8.8 > 5$, so the CLT applies.

* The mean of $\hat{p}$ is $p = 0.912$, and its standard error is
  $\sigma_{\hat{p}} = \sqrt{0.912 \times 0.088/100} \approx `r fmt(se_ft, 3)`$.
* About 95% of the time, $\hat{p}$ falls within $0.912 \pm 2(0.028)$, between
  **0.856 and 0.968**: somewhere between about 86 and 97 makes out of 100.

### Example: a tournament's average

Goals per World Cup match follow a Poisson distribution with $\lambda = 2.69$ (Week 7), so a single
match has $\mu = \lambda = 2.69$ and $\sigma = \sqrt{2.69} \approx `r fmt(sqrt(lam), 2)`$ goals. A
tournament's average over its 64 matches is a sample mean with $n = 64$, so by the CLT it is
approximately normal with mean 2.69 and standard error

$$\sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{`r fmt(sqrt(lam), 2)`}{\sqrt{64}} \approx `r fmt(se_wc, 3)`$$

* About 95% of tournaments, at this scoring rate, average between $2.69 \pm 2(0.205)$: **2.28 to 3.10**
  goals per match.
* The 2018 World Cup averaged $169/64 = 2.64$ goals per match. Surprising? No: 2.64 is well inside
  2.28 to 3.10.

A single match can easily have 0 goals or 6; a tournament's average is far more predictable. That is
the law of large numbers and the CLT working together: the average settles near $\mu$, and the CLT
says how near.

We can also find any other probability about $\bar{x}$, exactly as we did for single observations
in Week 6, as long as we standardize with the **standard error** instead of $\sigma$. How likely is a
tournament that averages **3 or more** goals per match?

$$z = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} = \frac{3 - 2.69}{0.205} \approx `r fmt(z3, 2)`,
\qquad P(\bar{x} \geq 3) = P(Z \geq `r fmt(z3, 2)`) = 1 - P(Z \leq `r fmt(z3, 2)`) \approx 1 - 0.934 = 0.066$$

About a 7% chance. (The exact answer, from the Poisson distribution of a tournament's total goals,
is also about 0.07: at $n = 64$ the normal approximation is very good.) The classic mistake is to
divide by $\sigma = 1.64$ instead of $\sigma/\sqrt{n} = 0.205$. That would describe a single
match, not a tournament's average.

# From an estimate to an interval

## Point estimates and interval estimates

Statistical inference draws conclusions about a population from sample data. It comes in two kinds,
**significance tests** (later in the course) and **estimation**, and estimation comes in two kinds as
well:

* A **point estimate** is a single statistic used to estimate a parameter: $\bar{x}$ for $\mu$,
  $\hat{p}$ for $p$, $s$ for $\sigma$.
* An **interval estimate** gives a range of plausible values for the parameter. The device we use is
  the **confidence interval**, which has the form
  $$\text{point estimate} \;\pm\; \text{margin of error}$$

A point estimate is almost never exactly right; the sampling distribution tells us it is usually
close. An interval says *how* close, with a stated level of confidence.

## Turning the probability statement around

In the last section we said

$$P\left(\mu - 2\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} \;\leq\; \bar{x} \;\leq\; \mu + 2\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right) \approx 0.95$$

But to say that $\bar{x}$ lies within two standard errors of $\mu$ is the same as saying that $\mu$
lies within two standard errors of $\bar{x}$. If you are within 2 miles of me, I am within 2 miles of
you. So, with a little algebra,

$$P\left(\bar{x} - 2\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} \;\leq\; \mu \;\leq\; \bar{x} + 2\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right) \approx 0.95$$

The interval $\bar{x} \pm 2\sigma/\sqrt{n}$ is a **95% confidence interval** for $\mu$. It needs only
things we know: the sample mean, $\sigma$ and $n$. (This week $\sigma$ is known; next week we replace
it with $s$, and look at confidence levels other than 95%.)

Read that last probability statement carefully. $\mu$ is a fixed number, not a random one. What is
random is the **interval**, because it is built from $\bar{x}$, and $\bar{x}$ changes from sample to
sample. The 95% describes the method: over all possible samples, about 95% of the intervals built this
way capture $\mu$.

## How often does an interval capture $\mu$?

Back to the songs, where we can cheat and check, because we know $\mu = `r fmt(MU, 2)`$. Below are 25
random samples of $n = 20$ songs. Each line is $\bar{x} \pm 2(0.34)$, the sample mean plus or minus
the margin of error:

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.height=4.5, fig.width=9, fig.align='center', fig.alt = "25 horizontal confidence intervals for mean song length, one per row, each a dot at the sample mean with a line 0.68 minutes either side, plus a vertical line at mu = 3.71 minutes. 24 of the intervals cross the vertical line. One interval, centered near 4.7 minutes, lies entirely to the right of it and is marked in red as a miss."}
ggplot(ci, aes(y = i)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = MU, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = lo, xend = hi, yend = i, color = hit), linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(aes(x = m, color = hit), size = 2) +
  annotate('text', x = MU + 0.04, y = 26.5, label = 'mu == 3.71', parse = TRUE, hjust = 0, size = 5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 'grey35', `FALSE` = 'red'),
                     labels = c(`TRUE` = 'Captures μ', `FALSE` = 'Misses μ'), name = NULL) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0.5, 27)) +
  labs(x = 'Song length (minutes)', y = 'Sample') +
  notes_theme + theme(legend.position = 'top', legend.text = element_text(size = 12),
                      axis.text.y = element_blank(), axis.ticks.y = element_blank())
```

`r sum(ci$hit)` of the 25 intervals capture $\mu$; one, from a sample whose mean happened to land far
to the right, misses. That is what "95% confident" means: about 95% of intervals made this way capture
the parameter.

> **A note on "about".** Repeat this 10,000 times and `r fmt(100 * cover, 0)`% of the intervals
> capture $\mu$, a little more than 95%. Song length has a handful of extremely long tracks, and with
> only $n = 20$ songs the sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$ is not yet quite normal (it is more
> peaked, with a long right tail), so the empirical rule is only approximate. This is the "if the
> population has extreme outliers, you may need more" caveat at work: for song length it takes
> samples of a couple of hundred before the rate settles near 95%.

### Example: an interval for mean song length

In practice we see only **one** sample, and we do not know $\mu$. Suppose our sample is the bottom
interval in the plot: $n = 20$ songs with $\bar{x} = 3.64$ minutes. With $\sigma = 1.51$ minutes,
$SE = 0.34$ minutes.

* The 95% confidence interval for $\mu$ is
  $$3.64 \pm 2(0.34) = 3.64 \pm 0.68, \qquad \text{from 2.96 to 4.32 minutes.}$$
* We would report it in the textbook's form: **"We estimate with 95% confidence that the mean length
  of all 18,860 songs is between 2.96 and 4.32 minutes."**
* Does it capture $\mu = 3.71$? Yes. But in real life we could not check.

## What "95% confident" does and does not mean

The **confidence level** is the probability that the interval will capture the parameter **before
the data are collected**. It is the long-run success rate of the method. Once the data are in and the
interval is computed, **the interval either does or does not contain the parameter**: there is
nothing random left, and we simply do not know which.

So for the interval 2.96 to 4.32 minutes:

* **Correct:** "If we took many samples of 20 songs and built an interval from each, about 95% of
  those intervals would capture the true mean song length."
* **Not correct:** "There is a 95% probability that $\mu$ is between 2.96 and 4.32." $\mu$ is a fixed
  number. It is either in this interval or it is not.
* **Not correct:** "95% of songs are between 2.96 and 4.32 minutes long." The interval is about the
  **mean** song length, not individual songs. (Individual songs vary by $\sigma = 1.51$ minutes, far
  more than this interval suggests.)

# Conclusion: what you should take away

## Sampling distributions

* A statistic is a random variable; its **sampling distribution** is its distribution over all
  possible samples of size $n$. Do not confuse it with the population distribution or the data
  distribution.
* For a small discrete population, build it by hand: list every sample (order matters), find each
  sample's probability, and add up the samples that give the same value.
* $\bar{x}$ has mean $\mu$ and standard error $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$; $\hat{p}$ has mean $p$ and standard
  error $\sqrt{p(1 - p)/n}$. Both shrink as $n$ grows; 4 times the sample halves the standard error.

## The central limit theorem

* For large $n$ (roughly $n \geq 30$, or $np$ and $n(1 - p)$ above 5 for a proportion), the sampling
  distribution of $\bar{x}$ or $\hat{p}$ is approximately normal, **whatever the shape of the
  population**. The population itself does not change.
* So a statistic falls within 2 standard errors of its parameter with probability about 0.95, and
  any other probability about $\bar{x}$ comes from $z = (\bar{x} - \mu)/(\sigma/\sqrt{n})$.

## Confidence intervals

* A **confidence interval** is point estimate $\pm$ margin of error. With the margin of error at
  2 standard errors, $\bar{x} \pm 2\sigma/\sqrt{n}$ is a 95% confidence interval for $\mu$.
* "95% confident" describes the method: about 95% of intervals built this way capture the parameter.
  Any one interval either does or does not.
